newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Analysts see little to cheer in S.Korean economy.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see little to cheer in S.Korean economy.

text.p: Despite the euphoria gripping the South Korean stock market, which hit a six-month closing high on Tuesday, economists said there was little to suggest the country's beleaguered economy had turned a corner.
"Technically it is still too early to say we have started to recover," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of the Daewoo Economic Research Institute.
Consumption, investment and capital imports were all too low, he said.
"Many big companies are facing the probability of bankruptcy and banks do not have a good attitude about making loans," Lee said. "It's a vicious circle."
But try telling that to Korean stock investors.
The Korea Composite Stock Price Index closed on Tuesday at its highest level since November 28, up 13.47 points, or 1.87 percent, to 734.67.
Blue chips, especially export-related companies, have led the market's climb as investors bet the yen's strength against the dollar would boost South Korea's exports and revive the lethargic economy.
The yen's value has a critical impact on the success of South Korea's major exports, including electronics goods and cars, which compete with Japanese products in world markets.
Given the edge Japanese products enjoy in quality and name recogition, South Korea's competitiveness hinges largely on price.

"The market anticipates events ahead of time," said Eugene Yun, managing director of Deutsche-Morgan Grenfell. "I think it's too early to say the Korean economy is recovering, but there are some encouraging signs."
Most encouraging is the current account deficit, which declined to $2.27 billion in March from $2.5 billion in February, though it was still up 142 percent from last year.

Foreign exchange reserves that have been hovering at low levels are now edging higher, and the won is strengthening against the dollar despite central bank intervention. The won closed on Tuesday at 890.60 after ending on Monday at 891.20.
Rising semiconductor exports, which account for nearly 20 percent of total exports, is also good news.
"There is evidence of a recovery in some areas, but there are a lot of negatives hanging out there," said Jonathan Dutton, deputy head of research at SBC Warburg.
Particularly frightenting is the spectre of corporate bankruptcies, analysts said.

Dainong, a small but high-profile conglomerate, or "chaebol", this week was the latest group to teeter towards failure. A bank committee opted to bail out the group as it did the much larger Jinro Group last month. Smaller companies have not been so lucky.
"A major failure of a big chaebol would hurt very much," said Yun.
Declining corporate bond yields are also cited as evidence of recovery. Three-year yields closed at 12.20 percent on Tuesday, compared to 12.33 percent a week earlier.
But Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd, a securities firm, described the drop in corporate bond yields as "modest" and said he was not yet impressed.
"It's an encouraging direction, of course, but it's not dramatic enough to get up and shout about," Morris said.
"I'm not a pessimist. I'm willing to believe things may be improving, but I'd like to see some evidence," he said.
Put the Federation of Korean Industries (FKI), the country's most influential business association, is in the "show-me" camp.

In a forecast released on Tuesday, FKI said it did not expect an economic turnaround any time soon. It cited sluggish investment, weak consumer demand and corporate cash-flow problems that had reduced demand.
"For all these reasons we cannot expect short-term economic recovery," the FKI statement said.
